title: Jonah and the Undertow
premise: Jonah Joubert, once a piano prodigy whose career ended in a scandal he has never explained, works nights as a janitor at the conservatory that expelled him. There he tends to Mireille Okonkwo-Bass, the last fluent speaker of Kavungu, a creole born of the port, who has been recording dying words in an empty practice room. When she asks him—of all people—to become her final student, Jonah must choose between the safety of his silence and the debt he owes to a truth about his teacher's death that only speaking Kavungu aloud can unlock. As Mireille fails and the conservatory moves to seize her recordings as institutional property, Jonah learns the language well enough to testify—to her, to the tribunal, and finally to himself—and the novel ends with him saying goodbye properly, out loud, in a language with one speaker left and one listener newly made.
about_author: Wendell Almeida is the pen name of a former conservatory custodian who spent eleven years sweeping the halls where he had once been a scholarship student. His fiction concerns the people institutions forget on purpose, and this is his third novel.

chapters.title: The Man Who Mops at Midnight
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Jonah. We follow his night shift through the conservatory: polishing floors under practice rooms, avoiding the portraits of faculty who remember him. He has a system for being unseen. The beat is quiet competence masking shame; establish his ritual of never entering Room 214.

chapters.title: Room 214
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He hears a voice after hours—an old woman reciting syllables into a recorder, words he doesn't know but that make his chest ache. He almost knocks. Instead he listens from the hallway and leaves before she finishes. Beat: longing disguised as trespass.

chapters.title: Three Years of Almost
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Jonah's POV. The scandal: his final recital, the accusation that he plagiarized his dead teacher Elias Joubert's unpublished compositions, the hearing he sat through without speaking. We learn he could have defended himself and chose not to. Beat: the wound explained but not yet healed.

chapters.title: Mireille
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, alternating to Mireille Okonkwo-Bass, ninety-one, who notices the janitor lingering outside her door. She was the conservatory's first archivist of port languages; now the university wants her office for offices. She begins leaving her door open on purpose. Beat: two watchers recognizing each other.

chapters.title: The Word for Sweep
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Mireille catches him emptying her bin and teaches him one word—kavungu itself means undertow, the pull beneath the water. She asks nothing. He practices it alone in the boiler room until it sounds right. Beat: first involuntary joy.

chapters.title: Inheritance Law
chapters.summary: POV: Dean Corliss-Hayes, the conservatory administrator, reviewing Mireille's contract. Her recordings are technically work-for-hire; her language belongs, on paper, to the institution. She plans a 'Legacy Initiative' press event. Beat: institutional appetite introduced politely.

chapters.title: Lessons Begin
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Mireille offers formally: one student, no fee, no records kept. He refuses twice; the third time she says in Kavungu the word for coward and he sits down. First real lesson—greetings, names, the way the language has no future tense, only intention. Beat: terror becoming commitment.

chapters.title: No Future Tense
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He learns the grammar: Kavungu speaks of tomorrow as 'the water coming.' He realizes the language cannot lie about time, which is why he avoided tenses in English too. Interleaved: he cleans Elias's old studio, untouched since the scandal. Beat: grief finding its grammar.

chapters.title: The Recordings
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. She inventories four hundred hours of tape: songs, courtship arguments, dockside curses, a lullaby in a mother tongue nobody else holds. She knows what the university will do with them—metadata, a plaque, silence. She begins choosing which tapes matter most. Beat: mortality as curatorial urgency.

chapters.title: Old Classmates
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A gala brings back Vivienne Marsh, now composer-in-residence, who testified against him three years ago. She is friendly, or performs friendliness. He mops around her heels. She mentions the Legacy Initiative; he says nothing, perfectly. Beat: the cost of invisibility made social.

chapters.title: What Elias Left
chapters.summary: Flashback, Jonah's POV. The fuller truth: Elias died mid-composition; Jonah finished the sonata from his sketches for a memorial concert, then let the board believe the worst rather than reveal that Elias had asked him to—and that doing so would expose Elias's stolen debts to Vivienne's family. Beat: loyalty revealed as the original sin.

chapters.title: The Water Coming
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Lessons deepen; Mireille makes him speak only Kavungu for whole hours. He tells her, badly, in her language, that he did something wrong once. She replies: 'The water does not apologize to the shore.' Beat: confession attempted, mercy deferred.

chapters.title: Legacy Initiative
chapters.summary: Corliss-Hayes's POV. The press event launches; Mireille is wheeled out as living heritage, photographed, thanked, and handed a non-assignment clause to sign. Jonah watches from behind the catering trays. Beat: the institution's love shown as acquisition.

chapters.title: The Lullaby Tape
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. She plays Jonah the lullaby her mother sang on the docks—the only surviving recording in the old deep register. She tells him who she'll leave it to, and looks at him while saying it. He deflects. Beat: inheritance offered and flinched from.

chapters.title: Vivienne's Visit
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. Curious about the janitor the archivist has adopted, she visits Room 214, hears Jonah answer Mireille in Kavungu, and recognizes the cadence of Elias's speech patterns. Suspicion kindles. Beat: the past acquiring witnesses.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Failure
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Mireille loses a word mid-lesson—a common one, the word for bread—and covers it with a joke. That night Jonah finds her sitting in the dark because she forgot how to turn on the lamp. Beat: decline acknowledged between them without naming it.

chapters.title: The Tribunal Notice
chapters.summary: Corliss-Hayes's POV. Legal informs her the Joubert estate dispute may reopen if new evidence surfaces; someone has requested the sealed hearing transcript. She orders it delayed. Beat: institutional self-protection as antagonist action.

chapters.title: Who Requested It
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. It was her request. She has found Elias's sketchbook in her late aunt's papers—with marginal notes in a hand she now suspects was Jonah's. She isn't sure whether she wants vindication or absolution. Beat: antagonist complicated into mirror.

chapters.title: Intermediate Silence
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Winter lessons; Mireille teaches him the honorific forms used for the dead, and he realizes she is teaching him how to speak to Elias. He composes—not music, sentences—in Kavungu, and reads them aloud to an empty studio. Beat: art reborn as language.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: Corliss-Hayes's POV. She offers Mireille a funded fellowship, a named archive, medical care—if Mireille signs over all rights and names the university her linguistic heir. Mireille asks for a night to think. Beat: temptation priced in dignity.

chapters.title: What Mireille Decides
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV. She signs—but crosses out one line, keeping the lullaby tape and 'whatever my student carries in his mouth.' Corliss-Hayes, not reading closely, files it. Beat: quiet victory inside surrender.

chapters.title: Discovery
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She confronts Jonah in the stairwell with the sketchbook. He neither denies nor explains; he answers in Kavungu, which infuriates her. She threatens to reopen the plagiarism case unless he tells her everything. Beat: the secret under formal threat.

chapters.title: Almost Saying It
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He drafts the truth three times—for Vivienne, for the dean, for Mireille—and burns none of them, keeps all three in his locker like unsent letters. Mireille finds him there at 3 a.m. and says, in Kavungu, 'Say it to me first.' Beat: the dam tested.

chapters.title: The Confession in Kavungu
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, mostly dialogue. He tells Mireille everything in her language—Elias's request, the debts, the silence, the shame. She listens without interrupting, then says the language has a verb form used only for carrying someone else's burden uphill. She conjugates it with his name. Beat: absolution earned, not given.

chapters.title: Stroke
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV, fragmenting syntax mirroring aphasia. Mid-lesson she reaches for the word for student and the room tilts. Hospital. Jonah holds her hand and speaks to her in Kavungu; her eyes track. Beat: crisis; the stakes become literal and bodily.

chapters.title: Visiting Hours
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The hospital allows fifteen minutes; the conservatory sends a card signed by everyone and no one. Jonah begins visiting daily, reading her the tapes' contents aloud so the words live in a second mouth. Nurses start calling him her grandson. Beat: devotion without status.

chapters.title: The Hearing Scheduled
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. She files to reopen the case, then immediately regrets it when she learns of Mireille's stroke. Corliss-Hayes, seeing PR risk, schedules the tribunal quietly for the last week of term. Beat: collision course set by three different motives.

chapters.title: What the Tapes Hold
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Listening to tape 311, he hears Elias's voice—young, recorded by Mireille decades ago—speaking Kavungu with the same phrasing Jonah inherited. Proof, of a kind, that what he carried was taught, not stolen. Beat: evidence arriving as grace.

chapters.title: Subpoena
chapters.summary: Corliss-Hayes's POV. The tribunal subpoenas the archive; lawyers discover Mireille's crossed-out line and declare the lullaby tape personally bequeathed—to a janitor. The dean summons Jonah. Beat: the hidden arrangement surfacing at the worst moment.

chapters.title: The Dean's Bargain
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Corliss-Hayes offers reinstatement, a studio, a public apology from the board—if he testifies that Elias's compositions were institutional property and hands over the sketchbook. Everything he lost, traded for the last lie. Beat: climax's temptation stated plainly.

chapters.title: Night Before
chapters.summary: Alternating short sections: Jonah cleaning the hall one last time; Vivienne rereading Elias's margins and understanding they were instructions, not theft; Mireille in the hospital asking a nurse to open the window 'so the water can come.' Beat: stillness before the break.

chapters.title: Tribunal
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The hearing room where he stayed silent three years ago. Asked to state his name, he answers in Kavungu first, then English, then tells the whole truth: Elias's request, the debts, his own cowardice, and what the sketchbook margins actually say. Beat: the long-deferred sentence finally spoken aloud.

chapters.title: Vivienne Rises
chapters.summary: Vivienne's POV. Called to respond, she confirms the margins match Elias's teaching style, withdraws her claim, and publicly apologizes for testifying on inference. The board scrambles; Corliss-Hayes goes pale. Beat: justice achieved outside the law's original frame, by testimony.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Institutional
chapters.summary: Corliss-Hayes's POV. Damage control: the Legacy Initiative reframed as 'the Okonkwo-Bass Living Archive,' Jonah offered a fellowship he doesn't want. She realizes she never once asked Mireille what the language meant to her. Beat: antagonist granted a bitter, human epiphany.

chapters.title: The Last Lesson
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Discharged home, Mireille gives their final lesson: not vocabulary but the farewell formula—words spoken only when you mean you won't see someone again. She makes him repeat it until it stops sounding like a spell and starts sounding like a promise. Beat: preparation for goodbye as the true curriculum.

chapters.title: Undertow
chapters.summary: Mireille's POV, lucid fragments. Night. She asks him to speak the farewell formula to her now, while she can hear it properly. He does—out loud, complete, unflinching. She corrects one vowel, smiles, and says the water is here. Beat: the goodbye done right; death met on the speaker's own terms.

chapters.title: One Speaker, One Listener
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. The funeral, small, in Kavungu and English both. The university claims its archive; Jonah claims tape 311 and the lullaby. Reporters ask if the language dies with her. He answers: 'It has one speaker left and one listener newly made.' Beat: grief converted into custody.

chapters.title: Recital
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Spring. He requests Room 214 for one evening, open doors, no program. He plays Elias's finished sonata and then speaks—in Kavungu—the story of Mireille, the docks, the lullaby, translating as he goes for a full house. Vivienne sits in the front row. Beat: return to the stage on his own terms; the prodigy's second debut.

chapters.title: The Student Becomes the Archive
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He takes a day job teaching a free Saturday class in the port district—dockworkers' grandchildren, curious teenagers—recording nothing, owning nothing, passing it mouth to mouth. Corliss-Hayes attends once, anonymously, and stays for the whole hour. Beat: inheritance redistributed outside institutional walls.

chapters.title: Out Loud
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, closing. Dawn at the harbor. He greets the water in Kavungu, uses the future-as-intention tense to describe what he will do next year, and says the farewell formula once more—not as an ending but as proof he can now say things properly, at last, out loud. Final image: the tide pulling, and him standing firm inside it. Beat: resolution; silence permanently broken.
